title: Shipton's Yeti Footprint
hook: In 1951, a mountaineer photographed a giant footprint high in the Himalayas.

beats.label: THE CASE
beats.line: Explorer Eric Shipton was scouting a route across the Menlung Glacier.

beats.label: CLUE 1
beats.line: At nineteen thousand feet, he found a huge footprint pressed into the snow.

beats.label: CLUE 2
beats.line: For scale, he placed his ice axe beside it, then took a photograph.

beats.label: CLUE 3
beats.line: The print showed five toes, twice the width of a normal human foot.

beats.label: THEORY
beats.line: Skeptics say a bear or wolf track simply melted wider in the sun.

beats.label: THE TWIST
beats.line: The photograph remains one of the most debated pieces of yeti evidence today.

end.line: Was it a bear track, or something stranger?

description: In 1951, explorer Eric Shipton photographed a huge footprint high on the Menlung Glacier. It remains one of the most famous, and most debated, pieces of yeti evidence.

facts.claim: In November 1951, mountaineer Eric Shipton photographed a large footprint-like impression on the Menlung Glacier during an Everest reconnaissance expedition.
The print was found at around 19,000 feet and Shipton placed an ice axe next to it for scale.
The photograph appears to show a large, roughly human-shaped print with what look like five toes.
Climbing partner Michael Ward also witnessed and photographed the print.
Skeptics have suggested the print could be an animal track, such as a fox or wolf, distorted by melting snow in sunlight.
The photograph remains one of the most widely reproduced pieces of purported yeti evidence.
